study_context.outcome: Alive and independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0-2) at 6 months
study_context.population: Acute ischemic stroke patients within 6 hours of symptom onset

hypothesis.title: Middle-aged patients (50–69) benefit moderately from alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients aged 50–69 receiving alteplase have a moderate increase in Alive & independent at 6 months compared with control.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Intermediate age group balances benefit of reperfusion with manageable hemorrhage risk.

hypothesis.mechanism: Adequate penumbral tissue with moderate comorbidity burden supports reperfusion benefit while limiting bleeding complications.
evidence_basis: Thrombolysis trial subgroup analyses indicating benefit across middle-aged adults
Clinical experience showing good functional recovery in this age group
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In patients aged 50–69, alteplase increases proportion OHS 0-2 at 6 months by 5–12% versus control.

hypothesis.title: Older patients (70–79) have lower net benefit but still positive
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients aged 70–79 derive a smaller but positive benefit from alteplase on Alive & independent at 6 months vs control.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Age-associated risks (bleeding, frailty) attenuate benefit but do not fully negate it in this bracket.

hypothesis.mechanism: Increased microangiopathy and comorbidity raise hemorrhage risk and reduce recovery potential, reducing absolute benefit of reperfusion.
evidence_basis: Older patient subgroup analyses from thrombolysis registries
Physiologic decline in recovery potential with age
hypothesis.testable_prediction: For age 70–79, alteplase produces a small absolute increase (2–6%) in OHS 0-2 at 6 months vs control.

hypothesis.title: Younger elderly (60–69) achieve best balance of benefit and safety
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients aged 60–69 achieve the highest net benefit-to-risk ratio from alteplase compared with other age bands.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: This decade often represents substantial salvageable brain with manageable comorbidity profile.

hypothesis.mechanism: Moderate age-related changes but preserved recovery potential and acceptable hemorrhage risk maximize net benefit.
evidence_basis: Clinical experience and subgroup summaries from registries
Physiologic rationale for preserved reserve in this age band
hypothesis.testable_prediction: For age 60–69, alteplase increases OHS 0-2 at 6 months by ≥8% compared to control.

hypothesis.title: Moderate NIHSS (5–14) achieve largest absolute benefit
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients with NIHSS 5–14 have the largest absolute improvement in Alive & independent at 6 months after alteplase versus control.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Moderate deficits represent substantial salvageable tissue where reperfusion yields meaningful functional gains.

hypothesis.mechanism: Optimal balance of significant penumbra with reasonable baseline recovery potential; benefit exceeds hemorrhagic risk.
evidence_basis: Meta-analyses showing robust benefit in moderate severity strokes
Trial data often showing greatest absolute benefit in this NIHSS range
hypothesis.testable_prediction: For NIHSS 5–14, alteplase increases OHS 0-2 at 6 months by ≥10% absolute vs control.

hypothesis.title: Low NIHSS (0–4) have limited absolute benefit from alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients with NIHSS 0–4 have a small absolute increase in Alive & independent at 6 months with alteplase compared with control; benefit may be minimal and risk may outweigh benefit in some cases.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Mild strokes often recover spontaneously; small absolute gain from reperfusion may not justify bleeding risk.

hypothesis.mechanism: Large proportion of mild stroke patients have rapid spontaneous recovery; thrombolysis bleeding risk may overshadow small gains.
evidence_basis: Trials and registries reporting small absolute benefit and higher relative bleeding concerns in mild strokes
Clinical practice debates about thrombolysis in minor stroke
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In NIHSS ≤4 subgroup, absolute increase in OHS 0-2 with alteplase ≤3% and symptomatic ICH risk may negate benefit.

hypothesis.title: Severe stroke (NIHSS �3e=�3e15) — reduced probability of independence and smaller absolute benefit from alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Among acute ischemic stroke patients with NIHSS �3e=�3e15 (severe deficits), IV alteplase will be associated with a lower probability of being alive and independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0-2) at 6 months than in patients with lower NIHSS; the absolute treatment benefit will be smaller and the net clinical benefit may be limited by higher risk of hemorrhagic complications.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: High baseline stroke severity reflects larger infarct burden and lower salvageable penumbra, reducing probability of good functional recovery; although thrombolysis can recanalize occlusions, the absolute increase in independence is likely smaller and the risk of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage is higher in this subgroup, so net benefit is expected to be low.

hypothesis.mechanism: Higher NIHSS indicates larger ischemic territory and greater clot burden with less viable penumbra; reperfusion may be less likely to restore sufficient tissue to produce independence and may increase risk of hemorrhagic transformation.
evidence_basis: Observational and trial subgroup analyses show lower rates of favorable outcome with increasing baseline NIHSS.
Pathophysiological rationale: larger strokes have greater infarct volume and less salvageable tissue.
Thrombolysis is effective across severities but absolute benefit (and risk of sICH) varies by baseline severity.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the IST-3 sample, participants with NIHSS �3e=�3e15 who received alteplase will have a lower absolute proportion achieving OHS 0-2 at 6 months compared with those with NIHSS 5-14, and the absolute treatment effect (alteplase vs control) within the NIHSS �3e=�3e15 subgroup will be small (e.g., substantially smaller than in the moderate NIHSS subgroup and possibly not statistically significant).

hypothesis.title: Very high weight (>=100 kg) reduces benefit of IV alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those with body weight >= 100 kg will have a lower probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0-2) at 6 months after IV alteplase compared with lighter patients, because dose capping at the absolute maximum dose may lead to lower mg/kg exposure and reduced efficacy.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Alteplase is dosed at 0.9 mg/kg with an absolute maximum (commonly 90 mg). Very heavy patients may receive a capped absolute dose that results in lower mg/kg exposure, plausibly reducing recanalization efficacy and functional recovery. Comorbidities more common with high weight may further blunt benefit.

hypothesis.mechanism: Dose-capping leads to suboptimal per-kilogram fibrinolytic exposure in very heavy patients, reducing the chance of vessel recanalization and subsequent functional recovery; concomitant obesity-related comorbidities may also worsen outcomes.
evidence_basis: Pharmacologic dosing rule for alteplase: 0.9 mg/kg with absolute maximum dose.
Biologic plausibility that lower per-kg exposure may reduce thrombolytic efficacy.
Observational studies and subgroup analyses suggesting altered outcomes in very high-weight patients after weight-based, capped dosing (conceptual/analogous evidence).
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the treated arm, the proportion with OHS 0-2 at 6 months will be lower for patients >=100 kg than for patients <100 kg; an interaction test will show a reduced treatment effect of alteplase in the >=100 kg subgroup.

hypothesis.title: Low weight (<60 kg) increases bleeding risk and reduces net benefit
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Acute ischemic stroke patients with body weight < 60 kg who receive IV alteplase within 6 hours will have a lower probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0-2) at 6 months compared with heavier patients, driven by higher symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and greater frailty/malnutrition.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Low body weight may mark frailty, malnutrition, or reduced physiologic reserve; although dosing is weight-based, these patients may have increased vulnerability to bleeding or complications that reduce net clinical benefit.

hypothesis.mechanism: Frailty and reduced physiologic reserve in low-weight patients increases susceptibility to hemorrhagic complications (including symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage) and poorer recovery, offsetting potential benefit from thrombolysis.
evidence_basis: Clinical observations that frailty and low BMI can be associated with worse outcomes after acute interventions.
Pathophysiologic plausibility linking low body mass and reduced reserve to higher complication rates.
Reports/analyses linking low weight or low BMI with adverse outcomes in other acute stroke treatment contexts (analogous evidence).
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Treated patients <60 kg will have higher rates of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and a lower proportion achieving OHS 0-2 at 6 months versus treated patients >=60 kg; treatment-by-weight interaction will indicate reduced or negative net benefit in the <60 kg subgroup.

hypothesis.title: Moderate weight (approximately 60–99 kg) derives greater benefit from alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients with body weight in the moderate range (approximately 60–99 kg) treated with IV alteplase within 6 hours will have a higher probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0-2) at 6 months compared with both low-weight (<60 kg) and very-high-weight (>=100 kg) patients, because they receive near-ideal per-kg dosing without dose-capping and are less likely to be frail.

subgroup_rule.description: Patients weighing approximately 60 to 99 kg (moderate weight range)

treatment_recommendation.rationale: This weight range avoids the extremes associated with under- or over-exposure: patients typically receive near-target mg/kg dosing (without hitting the absolute cap) and are less likely to be frail, maximizing the chance of effective thrombolysis and good recovery.

hypothesis.mechanism: Appropriate per-kilogram alteplase exposure in the moderate weight range produces effective fibrinolysis with a favorable balance between recanalization and bleeding risk; lower prevalence of frailty/comorbidity supports better recovery.
evidence_basis: Pharmacologic dosing principles indicating optimal per-kg exposure in non-capped weight ranges.
Clinical plausibility that avoidance of extremes (very low or capped high weights) yields better net outcomes.
Analogous subgroup findings in thrombolytic/antithrombotic literature where mid-range weights show favorable benefit-risk.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Among treated patients, the highest proportion achieving OHS 0-2 at 6 months will be observed in those with weight 60–99 kg; statistical comparison will show superior treatment effect in this moderate-weight subgroup versus <60 kg and >=100 kg groups.

hypothesis.title: Marked hyperglycaemia (glucose >= 10) attenuates benefit of IV alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: In acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, admission glucose >= 10 is associated with reduced probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0-2) at 6 months following IV alteplase compared with patients with lower glucose, and the relative benefit of alteplase versus control is smaller in this subgroup.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Marked hyperglycaemia at presentation is plausibly associated with larger infarct growth, higher risk of haemorrhagic transformation and worse functional outcomes; this may blunt the net benefit of thrombolysis and could increase harm.

hypothesis.mechanism: Acute hyperglycaemia increases anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis in ischemic tissue, exacerbates blood–brain barrier disruption and oxidative stress, and raises risk of haemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion, reducing salvagable penumbra and diminishing thrombolysis benefit.
evidence_basis: Observational studies linking admission hyperglycaemia to larger infarct size and worse functional outcomes after ischemic stroke
Preclinical data showing hyperglycaemia worsens ischemic neuronal injury and increases haemorrhagic conversion after reperfusion
Clinical recommendations to correct marked hyperglycaemia in acute stroke because of potential harm
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the trial dataset, patients with admission glucose >= 10 who received alteplase will have a smaller absolute and relative increase in OHS 0-2 at 6 months compared with control than patients with glucose < 10; absolute treatment effect in the >=10 group will be ≤ the effect in the <10 group (possibly null or negative).

hypothesis.title: Hypoglycaemia (glucose < 4) predicts poor outcome and increases risk if thrombolysis administered before correction
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Acute hypoglycaemia (admission glucose < 4) is associated with lower likelihood of being alive and independent at 6 months and may increase risk of adverse outcomes if alteplase is given before glucose is corrected; thus immediate correction of hypoglycaemia is necessary and treatment benefit of alteplase is uncertain until glucose is normalized.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Hypoglycaemia itself can produce neurological deficits, worsen ischemic injury, and confound eligibility for thrombolysis; administering alteplase prior to correcting low glucose may be futile or harmful, so benefit of immediate alteplase is unlikely without glucose correction.

hypothesis.mechanism: Low blood glucose causes neuronal energy failure and may mimic or worsen ischemic injury; it can increase vulnerability to reperfusion injury and complicate neurological assessment, making thrombolysis unsafe or less effective until euglycaemia is restored.
evidence_basis: Guidelines and clinical practice recommending correction of hypoglycaemia before thrombolytic therapy
Case reports and small series where hypoglycaemia produced stroke-mimics and poor outcomes when not corrected
Physiological studies showing neuronal injury during hypoglycaemia
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Among trial participants with glucose < 4, those who received alteplase without documented prior correction will have lower rates of OHS 0-2 and higher adverse event rates at 6 months than comparable patients with glucose ≥ 4; correcting glucose prior to treatment will be associated with better outcomes.

hypothesis.title: Moderate hyperglycaemia (glucose 6–9) does not reduce — and may preserve — benefit from IV alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients with moderate admission hyperglycaemia (glucose in the 6–9 range) retain a clinically meaningful benefit from IV alteplase (higher probability of OHS 0-2 at 6 months) that is similar to or modestly greater than that seen in normoglycaemic patients.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Moderate elevation may reflect a stress response with salvageable penumbra and not yet the deleterious metabolic milieu of marked hyperglycaemia; thus benefit from reperfusion may be preserved and these patients should not be excluded from thrombolysis on this basis alone.

hypothesis.mechanism: A moderate stress-related rise in glucose may be a marker of acute physiological response without sufficient metabolic derangement to substantially worsen reperfusion injury; timely reperfusion can still salvage at-risk tissue leading to improved functional outcome.
evidence_basis: Observational analyses suggesting a graded relationship between admission glucose and outcome, with most pronounced harm at high levels
Studies reporting that mild–moderate hyperglycaemia is common and not uniformly predictive of poor thrombolysis response
Physiological rationale that deleterious effects increase with higher glucose levels
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the trial, patients with admission glucose 6–9 will show an absolute treatment effect (difference in proportion with OHS 0-2 between alteplase and control) that is comparable to or larger than that seen in patients with glucose 4–5.9, and substantially better than the effect observed in the >=10 group.

hypothesis.title: Higher baseline GCS (>=13) predicts greater benefit from IV alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Among acute ischemic stroke patients within 6 hours, those with baseline gcs_score_rand >= 13 will derive greater benefit from IV alteplase (higher probability of being alive and independent at 6 months) compared with patients with lower GCS.

subgroup_rule.description: Patients with GCS 13 or higher (mild or no impairment of consciousness).

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Higher GCS indicates preserved consciousness and likely smaller infarct / less severe neurological compromise, increasing the probability that reperfusion will salvage tissue and translate into functional independence. Lower baseline mortality and lower hemorrhagic complication rates in more alert patients may increase net benefit of thrombolysis.

hypothesis.mechanism: Preserved level of consciousness (GCS >=13) reflects less extensive brain injury and greater salvageable penumbra; reperfusion with alteplase is more likely to restore function without precipitating catastrophic hemorrhage.
evidence_basis: Level of consciousness correlates inversely with infarct size and overall stroke severity.
Patients with higher baseline neurological status have better absolute outcomes and lower complication rates after reperfusion therapies.
Clinical trials and registries suggest better functional recovery in less comatose patients treated with thrombolysis.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In this dataset, the odds ratio for being alive and independent at 6 months comparing alteplase vs control will be >1.5 in the subgroup with gcs_score_rand >= 13, and the absolute risk difference will be clinically meaningful (e.g., >8%).

hypothesis.title: Low baseline GCS (<=8) identifies patients with limited or harmful response to IV alteplase
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients with baseline gcs_score_rand <= 8 (severely depressed consciousness) will have little to no benefit or net harm from IV alteplase, with higher rates of poor outcome and hemorrhagic complications.

subgroup_rule.description: Patients with GCS 8 or lower (severe impairment/coma).

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Severely reduced consciousness often reflects large infarcts or mass effect and is associated with high baseline mortality; reperfusion in this setting may increase risk of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage and not restore meaningful independence, producing net harm.

hypothesis.mechanism: Severe depressed consciousness indicates extensive brain injury and blood–brain barrier disruption; thrombolysis may precipitate hemorrhagic transformation in large infarcts and is less likely to improve clinical status.
evidence_basis: Low GCS is associated with large infarct volume, raised intracranial pressure, and worse outcomes.
Observed higher rates of hemorrhagic transformation and death among comatose stroke patients receiving reperfusion therapies.
Clinical reasoning and registry data often exclude profoundly comatose patients from aggressive reperfusion due to poor expected benefit.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the subgroup with gcs_score_rand <= 8, the alteplase arm will show either no improvement or worse rates of independence at 6 months compared with control, and a higher incidence of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (relative increase vs control).

hypothesis.title: Fully alert patients (GCS == 15) have limited absolute benefit from alteplase due to ceiling effects
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients with baseline gcs_score_rand == 15 (fully alert) will have a smaller absolute benefit from IV alteplase for achieving independence at 6 months compared with patients with some impairment, because many already have a high probability of good outcome without treatment.

subgroup_rule.description: Patients who are fully alert (GCS exactly 15).

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Complete preservation of consciousness often reflects milder strokes with favorable prognosis; although relative treatment effect may exist, the absolute gain from alteplase is likely small (ceiling effect), making net clinical value uncertain when balancing hemorrhage risk.

hypothesis.mechanism: When baseline functional prospects are already favorable, reperfusion yields small incremental gains in independence; the risk of hemorrhage may offset small absolute benefits.
evidence_basis: Patients with minimal impairment commonly achieve good outcomes without intervention, reducing absolute risk reduction from active treatments.
Trial subgroup analyses frequently report smaller absolute benefit in patients with mild deficits despite possible relative effects.
Clinical equipoise often exists for very mild strokes regarding thrombolytic therapy because of the trade-off between small benefit and hemorrhage risk.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Among patients with gcs_score_rand == 15, the absolute difference in proportions alive and independent at 6 months between alteplase and control will be small (e.g., <5%) and not statistically significant in this sample.
